# Read-Capability Routing

The planner picks an executor because it thinks one is better suited. That preference is overridden
whenever the subtask must read something the chosen executor cannot open. **Capability beats
preference**, and it is checked before the run rather than discovered by it — sending a PDF to
something that cannot open one costs a full CLI round-trip and comes back as an apology.

## The two tables

Files are classified into read classes by extension, and each executor declares the classes it can
handle:

```python
READ_CLASSES = ("text", "extract", "vision")

AGENT_READS = {
    "claude": {"text", "extract", "vision"},
    "codex":  {"text"},
    ROUTER_AGENT: set(),
}
```

A fourth class, `opaque`, is what nothing can read — a binary, a compiled artifact — and naming it is
useful precisely because it routes to no one and should be reported, not attempted.

[[codex-cli]]'s entry is conservative on purpose: text is what it is established to handle here, and
anything else is a guess whose wrong answer costs a whole attempt. The router's empty set is not a
limitation to fix — it is [[openrouter]] being a bare chat completion with no file access, which is
the same fact the security model leans on.

## The bug this shape hides

`_sanitize` computes `need ⊄ AGENT_READS[agent]` and reroutes to the first fallback candidate that
can cover `need`. Since `reads` defaults to `["text"]` and the router's capability is `set()`, the
condition is true for *every* router-assigned subtask — including the pure-reasoning ones the planner
deliberately kept on the router because they read nothing at all. Every one of them was silently
moved to a CLI.

That made the last entry of the fallback order dead code, and the visible symptom appeared only in
the worst case: with both CLI subscriptions spent, a run reported that every capable agent had failed
while the router sat there, tool-free and perfectly able to answer. Fixed in 0.7.1 — a subtask that
declares no file reads stays where it was put. See [[agent-orchestrator]].

The general lesson is narrower than "test your predicates": a default value (`["text"]`) and an empty
capability set produce a rule that is *always* true, and a rule that is always true reads exactly like
a rule that works.
